AI scams aimed at older people, and how little we know about stopping them; the cybersecurity radar.
TECH RADAR
AI-powered scams target older people, and defences have not been tested where it matters
No. 8 · Thursday 29 October 2026 · Cybersecurity · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1A review of 63 studies finds that no AI scam detector has been tested with older people in real life, while their reported losses in the US reached $7.7 billion in 2025.
2At Politecnico di Milano, researchers catalogue 55 new tricks malware uses to hide from analysts; debuggers counter only 27% of them.
3Cybersecurity radar: the fastest growth is in attacks on AI itself, and new GitHub projects on prompt injection grew almost twelvefold in a year.
394
new cybersecurity papers today
+33%
research share of cybersecurity compared with 3 years ago
+1,069%
new GitHub projects on prompt injection, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
AI against scams targeting older adults: what works, and what has never been tested
Information · 25 October · review · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Bálint Vörös, Cecília Sik-Lányi · University of Pannonia (Hungary) · Cecília Sik-Lányi, h-index 22
Context. Scams aimed at older people now use generative AI: a cloned voice of a grandchild asking for money, a fake video of a bank employee, messages written by a chatbot that sound perfectly natural. Many hope AI itself can spot these frauds.
The authors reviewed 992 records and kept 63 studies. Adults aged 60 and over reported losses of $7.7 billion to the FBI in 2025, 59% more than in 2024. Most studies only measured what older people knew or intended to do after a training course; where real detection was measured, results were mixed and often null. No study tested an AI scam detector with older users in everyday life, and the only test of voice-deepfake detectors on older speakers found that their error rate roughly doubled. The authors propose a six-layer protection framework, not yet validated. It is today's signal because it shows a gap between the threat, already large, and defences that have not been tested on the people most at risk.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · CYBERSECURITY
Malware detectiongrowing
Research share +27% in 3 years · 1,750 papers in 2025
What it is about. To understand a suspicious program, analysts run it in a 'sandbox', an isolated computer, or step through it with a debugger. Malware often notices it is being watched and behaves innocently.
Evasion Games: Dissecting Malware Evasive Techniques Across Packers, Sandboxes, and Debuggers
ACM Transactions on Privacy and Security · 26 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Daniele Mammone and 5 others · Politecnico di Milano (Italy) · among the authors Stefano Zanero, h-index 34
WHAT THEY DOThey update the catalogue of hiding tricks with 55 newly documented methods, check how many of them are built into 25 tools that disguise programs, and test 7 online sandboxes and 4 debuggers against them.
RESULTSandboxes cope better with tricks that detect debugging or virtual machines but are still fooled by others, especially timing-based ones; debuggers counter only 27% of the evasions.
WHY IT MATTERSThe tools defenders rely on to study malware have blind spots that attackers can already exploit.
Network security and intrusion detectionstrong growth
Research share +81% in 3 years · 9,738 papers in 2025
What it is about. Intrusion detection systems watch network traffic to spot attacks, like a burglar alarm for a company's network.
An Explainable Hybrid Feature Selection Framework for Deep Learning-Based Intrusion Detection
Applied Sciences · 27 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Martins O. Onuorah, Yanxia Sun, Daniel J. Mashao · University of Johannesburg (South Africa), Kigali Independent University (Rwanda) · Yanxia Sun, h-index 44
WHAT THEY DOA system that first discards the least useful traffic characteristics, keeps a compact set, and then explains each alarm by showing which characteristics triggered it.
RESULTOn two public datasets it cuts the characteristics from 80 to 23 and from 86 to 15. Its balanced accuracy score (F1, from 0 to 1) is 0.833 and 0.992, better than the same model using all characteristics.
WHY IT MATTERSLighter, explainable alarms are cheaper to run and easier for security staff to trust.
Web application securitystrong growth
Research share +62% in 3 years · 1,264 papers in 2025
What it is about. Penetration testing means attacking your own systems, with permission, to find weaknesses before criminals do. It is slow, expensive work done by specialists.
Agentic and generative AI for intelligent autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing: A systematic analysis
Computer Science Review · 24 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Samuel Roy Anthony Truss and 6 others · Keele University, University of Liverpool (United Kingdom), University of Jordan (Jordan)
WHAT THEY DOA systematic review of how AI agents and language models are used to automate security audits, from 1,144 records down to 72 studies, ending with a reference model for trustworthy automated auditing.
WHY IT MATTERSAccording to the review, research is still fragmented and focused on office IT, while factories and infrastructure are left behind: a gap to close before trusting AI 'auditors'.
Cryptography and data securitygrowing
Research share +27% in 3 years · 3,310 papers in 2025
What it is about. Fully homomorphic encryption lets a computer work on data while it stays encrypted: a hospital could have an AI analyse records without the AI provider ever seeing them.
Machine learning over encrypted data: a survey of fully homomorphic encryption for AI systems
Artificial Intelligence Review · 26 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Dillon Davidson and 4 others · University of Nevada, Las Vegas (United States), University of Bristol (United Kingdom) · among the authors Rasheed Hussain, h-index 40
WHAT THEY DOA survey of how AI models, from classic algorithms to the transformers behind chatbots, are adapted to run on encrypted data, with a map of the trade-offs between accuracy, speed and security.
WHY IT MATTERSA good entry point to a technology that could make AI usable on health and financial data without exposing it; speed is still the main obstacle.
RADAR OF THE DAY · CYBERSECURITY
What it is about. Protecting computers, networks and data from attacks: from phishing emails and ransomware to attacks on AI systems themselves, such as prompt injection, hidden instructions that trick a chatbot or an AI agent into doing something it should not.

Spam and phishing detection

▲ +80%
Privacy-preserving technologies
using personal data without exposing people

What developers and the public do
SIGNALGITHUB
(year on year)		HACKER NEWS
(year on year)
«prompt injection»▲ +1,069%■ +5%
«llm security»▲ +677%▼ −9%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (93 and 65 in the quarter). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views up for prompt injection (+52%), down for ransomware (−18%) and post-quantum cryptography (−15%). Adoption data cover only AI-related security; data updated 27 October. Since this week, quantum physics papers are no longer counted in this vertical.
In short: Research, developers and the public agree: the security of AI itself is the fastest-moving front, while classic topics such as ransomware draw less attention than a year ago.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Deepfake — a fake video, photo or voice made with AI, such as the cloned voice of a relative asking for money.
Sandbox — an isolated computer where suspicious software can be run safely, like a sealed room for examining a parcel.
Prompt injection — hidden instructions placed in a text, web page or file that trick an AI into ignoring its rules.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on robotics and automation. Worth watching: field trials of AI scam detectors with older users, the missing piece identified by today's signal.

Two of today's papers are reviews and summarise others' work. A journal's quality does not guarantee that results are correct.
